picked.t: Vietnamese woman quits $7,700-a-month job to open vegetarian restaurant
picked.body: Diep, 57, spends most of her time at the two Ho Chi Minh City branches of her restaurant, Shamballa. She oversees the kitchen, interacts with staff and customers, and develops vegetarian products for home cooking. The epiphany came in the summer of 2012 during her second trip to Tibet, when she suffered a severe health crisis. She experienced shortness of breath, facial swelling, and a squeezing sensation in her head. For nearly three weeks, she relied on oxygen masks and care from local monks and nuns, who provided intravenous drips and nourishment. "There were times I thought I wouldn't survive," she says. Before the trip, she had spent years working at large corporations. She was accustomed to long meetings, overseas business trips, and a senior management job that fetched her over VND200 million a month. She had a lifestyle many people would have given an arm and a leg for, but her days bedridden in Tibet made her truly understand human fragility and its limits against illness. "I suddenly realized that such a high salary means nothing in the face of death." Returning to Vietnam, she continued her office job, business trips, and familiar pace of life, but her perspective on life had changed irreversibly. She switched to a strict vegetarian diet and paid more attention to meditation and things that had previously been overshadowed by work. Research shows that a near-death experience can change how people view life, leading them to appreciate nature, care for others, and better understand the meaning of life. It can also change diets. A 2023 review study by Tani Khara of Australia's University of Technology Sydney claimed there were eight cases where individuals switched from eating meat to a vegetarian or plant-based diet following a near-death experience. During her early years as a vegetarian, Diep struggled to find meals that suited her palate. She liked noodle soups, but many vegetarian restaurants failed to meet her flavor expectations. As a result, she went into the kitchen and experimented with ingredients, looking for ways to make dishes that were both delicious and visually appealing. She wanted to make vegetarian foods good enough for carnivores not to sniff at. More than a month after starting her vegetarian diet, a staff member offered her a meat-filled fried spring roll at a company conference party in Hanoi. Diep accepted and took a bite. She immediately felt ashamed for breaking her commitment to herself. "If I could not overcome such a small temptation, how could I achieve great things?" she says about that episode. After that, she gave up meat completely. In 2015, during a three-week pilgrimage in India, she first told her meditation teacher about her desire to open a restaurant. But she did not want a place exclusively for vegetarians; she wanted the food to be tasty and beautiful enough to attract non-vegetarians as well. The teacher told her that if she wanted to do it, he would support her. The idea stayed in her mind for a few more years. She continued her corporate job but paid close attention to the food, preparation methods, ambiance, and diner experience whenever she ate out. One morning in 2018, she woke up and realized things had changed: "I suddenly woke up and didn't want to do office work for another minute. I just wanted to open a vegetarian restaurant." Her superiors did not want her to quit, suggesting she should take a few months of unpaid leave to think it over. The position would be hers if she wanted to return, they promised. But after those few months passed, she did not want to go back. This time, she chose the restaurant. Friends called her "crazy," while her family respected her choice. Later, the same friends who had questioned her decision helped her during the early days of her business. In May 2019, Diep opened her first vegetarian restaurant on Trinh Van Can Street in Ho Chi Minh City. She named it Shamballa, referring to a concept in Tibetan philosophy representing a realm of peace without suffering. The name was redolent of the trip that changed her perspective on life. She wanted the restaurant to be a place where diners could temporarily escape the outside pace of life and enjoy a meal in a quiet space. In the early days, business was good, with the restaurant attracting lots of foreign tourists. At times, people had to book tables in advance. She then opened a new, larger, and more convenient branch in the downtown area. But just seven months after the first restaurant opened, the Covid-19 pandemic broke out. Business plummeted, but the restaurant had to pay staff and for operating costs. Diep had to dip into her savings. "I almost emptied my savings, and even had to borrow from friends," she says. Colleagues and former bosses asked her to return to the office, but she refused. Whenever under pressure, Diep remembered the words of her meditation teacher: that if she could help 10 people have a vegetarian meal without the killing of animals, she would cr

The third most visited country in Southeast Asia after Malaysia and Thailand welcomed nearly 16 million international visitors in the first eight months of 2026, up 14.4% year-on-year, driving up demand across hotels, travel companies, transport, restaurants and tourist attractions. A 2026 survey by Hoteljob.vn found that nearly 90% of tourism businesses planned to recruit. In Ho Chi Minh City alone, 89.7% of businesses were hiring, while 71.8% said recruitment was difficult or very difficult. The biggest shortages were among frontline workers, particularly in housekeeping, engineering, food service, front-office operations, and kitchens. The Politburo's Resolution dated Aug. 22, along with the government's action programme adopted on Sept. 7, set the target for tourism to directly contribute 10-12% of GDP by 2030, attracting 45-50 million international visitors and generate total revenue of US$80-90 billion. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, and Da Nang are envisioned as major tourism growth hubs, while Phu Quoc emerges as a new hub. These targets will place greater demands on the tourism workforce, not only in terms of numbers but also skills, from frontline workers and foreign-language guides to managers, technology specialists and professionals delivering high-end services. Ho Chi Minh City's tourism sector, for example, is facing gaps in supervisory and management positions, as businesses seek staff capable of operating in an increasingly digitalized, international and competitive environment. Foreign-language tour guides are another weak link. Demand is rising rapidly from markets such as Russia and India, while arrivals from Europe and the Middle East are also increasing. Yet training guides with the language skills and cultural knowledge needed to serve these markets can take years. The labor crunch is even more acute in destinations far from major urban centers. In Con Dao, hotels and resorts regularly struggle to recruit receptionists, housekeepers, chefs, and service staff, while travel companies face shortages of sales, marketing, and tour guide staff. Higher salaries have done little to solve the problem. The island's high cost of living and distance from the mainland make it difficult to attract and retain skilled workers, with many leaving after only a few months. According to Hoteljob.vn, 79.5% of tourism businesses have raised salaries or improved benefits over the past year. Yet 59.2% cited lower incomes compared with other industries as a key reason young people leave the profession, while limited career prospects were another major factor. Experts say Vietnam's tourism labor shortage is not simply about training more people. The bigger challenge is narrowing the gap between what schools teach and what employers need. Nearly 80% of businesses surveyed said fewer than 20% of young applicants could start work immediately, while more than 84% said new recruits needed at least a month before they could work independently. Employers are also increasingly concerned with workplace discipline, service mindset and the ability to work under pressure, rather than technical skills alone. Experts say stronger links with policymakers, training institutions and businesses are needed to better forecast demand, redesign training and give young workers clearer career paths. Vietnam's tourism goals will require a workforce to match. If training and retention continue to lag behind visitor growth, the industry's labor shortage could become one of its biggest bottlenecks on the road to 2030.

picked.t: Man killed in HCMC after falling tree branch crushes motorbike during thunderstorm
picked.body: Le Van Dung and his wife, 57-year-old Duong Thi Thoan, were heading home from work along An Duong Vuong Street at around 6:30 p.m. when the tragedy struck. As they passed the Ho Chi Minh City University of Education in Cho Quan Ward, a massive tree branch broke in the strong winds and heavy rain , striking their vehicle and throwing them onto the road. The fallen branch, measuring approximately 30 cm in diameter, brought down a canopy large enough to completely block one traffic lane. The couple was transported to An Binh Hospital, about 1.2 km from the scene. Dung succumbed to his severe injuries shortly after arrival. Cho Quan Ward Chairman Nguyen Vo Xuan Ky confirmed that the wife sustained spinal trauma alongside multiple other injuries. She was later transferred to Cho Ray Hospital for treatment. Local authorities have visited the hospital to offer support to her and her family, he said, adding that the ward will formally request the local tree management agency to urgently inspect the area's canopy to prevent further tragedies. Prior to the recent expansion of HCMC's administrative boundaries to include Binh Duong and Vung Tau, official statistics recorded more than 200,000 trees lining over 1,200 city roads. Roughly 7,600 of these trees stand 20 to 50 meters tall, primarily concentrated in central districts. Many are decades-old dipterocarp and Hopea trees, distinguished by their large trunks and heavy branches, which pose a significant risk of breaking or uprooting during severe weather. An Duong Vuong Street is heavily shaded by these towering old-growth dipterocarps, known for their straight trunks and dense, year-round green foliage. However, the thoroughfare has a deadly track record regarding falling debris. In September 2024, a 20-cm-thick dipterocarp branch fell from nearly 20 m near the same university, killing a 52-year-old woman. Eight years earlier, in 2016, a dipterocarp measuring over 30 m tall and a meter in diameter was uprooted during heavy rain on the street, crushing a 25-year-old man who later died from his injuries.

picked.t: Patients pack Ho Chi Minh City's largest hospital from dawn as daily visits top 10,000
picked.body: Patients wait to see doctors at Cho Ray Hospital on Sept. 15. Reception counters at the hospital, the largest in southern Vietnam, begin issuing queue numbers at 4:30 a.m., leaving waiting halls packed before doctors started consultations at 6 a.m. Patient volumes at the hospital have jumped sharply since the beginning of this month. Dr. Le Trung Nhan, head of the Outpatient Department, said the facility typically receives 8,000 to 9,000 patient visits per day, with figures exceeding 10,000 on some days such as Sept. 7. Automatic ticket kiosks and reception counters remain heavily frequented, though conditions have eased over the past year following the introduction of an app-based appointment registration system that cuts down on early morning queues. More than 70% of patients now schedule visits in advance via the app, requiring them only to print their queue numbers upon arrival before heading straight to consultation rooms. To help manage the flow, personnel from the hospital's Social Work Department and a team of volunteers, primarily university students, deploy early each morning to guide and support arriving patients. This sustained influx is largely fueled by individuals requiring routine check-ups for chronic illnesses, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and organ transplants. Overall, follow-up examinations account for roughly 60% of all patient traffic. With seating rows completely filled, 65-year-old Thu leaned against a pillar waiting for her turn outside the examination room after an early morning arrival. She reached the hospital at 5 a.m. following a more than four-hour bus journey from Bao Loc in Lam Dong Province near Da Lat, to HCMC. Thu had been experiencing persistent headaches, lightheadedness, dizziness, and numbness in both legs for several months. picked.t: 10 best fine dining restaurants in Southeast Asia
picked.body: Koma Singapore topped the list for the second consecutive year in Tripadvisor's 2026 Travelers' Choice Best of the Best Restaurants Awards, based on an analysis of reviews from the travel platform's users. The restaurant at Marina Bay Sands serves modern Japanese cuisine, combining ingredients sourced from Japan with contemporary influences. Guests enter through a 20-meter passageway lined with glowing vermillion arches inspired by Kyoto's Fushimi Inari Shrine before arriving at an atmospheric bar. The Rhythms Restaurant in Hanoi ranked second. Located on the seventh floor of La Sinfonía del Rey Hotel & Spa in downtown Hanoi, it has an outdoor dining area overlooking Hoan Kiem Lake and the Old Quarter. The restaurant serves fine-dining dishes, cocktails and wine. Its west-facing terrace also offers views of the sunset over the city. Kroya by Chef Chanrith , at Shinta Mani Angkor in Cambodia's Siem Reap, ranked third. It serves modern Cambodian cuisine inspired by traditional Khmer recipes. The restaurant uses local ingredients and contemporary cooking techniques. Its lunch menu features à la carte dishes, while dinner is offered as a set menu highlighting seasonal flavors. Diners can choose between the indoor dining area and open-air swing tables. The restaurant is open to both hotel guests and outside visitors. Boy'N'Cow on the popular tourist island Bali in Indonesia, a dry-aged meat restaurant and cocktail lounge specializing in beef aged on site, secured the fourth place. The restaurant uses ingredients sourced from different countries and prepares its dishes from scratch, Tripadvisor wrote. Its menu features share-style dishes alongside handcrafted cocktails, served in an industrial-style setting with an upbeat atmosphere. Dava , an Argentine-inspired restaurant with panoramic ocean views beside the AYANA Villas Lobby in Indonesia, ranked fifth. The restaurant focuses on Argentina's asado barbecue tradition, serving beef cuts and line-caught seafood cooked over a wood-fired grill. Its menu includes Wagyu steaks, Latin-inspired dishes and seafood preparations. It also offers South American-inspired cocktails, a selection of wines and house-made desserts. Diners can choose between the open-air setting and ocean views, particularly around sunset. At sixth position, Henshin is a Peruvian-Japanese restaurant and rooftop bar on levels 67-69 of The Westin Jakarta, making it one of the city's highest dining venues. The restaurant specializes in Nikkei cuisine, combining Japanese and Peruvian culinary influences under the direction of a Peruvian chef. Its dining areas and rooftop bar offer panoramic views of Jakarta's skyline. Bai Yun , a Chinese hot-pot restaurant in Nusa Dua, Indonesia, ranked seventh. Its name means "white cloud" in Mandarin, referring to the steam rising from the hot pot, which resembles clouds. The restaurant offers a selection of fresh ingredients and sauce combinations. Benjarong , included in the 2026 Michelin Guide for the Philippines, came in 8th. It serves traditional Thai cuisine with a modern approach, combining time-honored cooking techniques with contemporary presentation. Summer Palace at Edsa Shangri-La of the Philippines ranked 9th. Located on the mezzanine level of the Tower Wing in Luzon, the restaurant serves Cantonese cuisine, with a menu of around 180 dishes featuring dim sum, seafood and noodles. It offers eight signature dishes and classics created by its culinary team. Smoking is not permitted. Finishing the top 10 were Thailand's Punjab Grill Bangkok which serves Indian cuisine with a focus on dishes from India's northwestern region, combining traditional recipes with contemporary interpretations. Led by Chef Bharath S. Bhat, the restaurant's menu includes vegetarian and non-vegetarian dishes, along with specialties such as crab and lentil shorba, avocado papdi chaat, tawa scallops and tandoori jheenga, Tripadvisor describes. Classic dishes include butter chicken, dal makhani and lamb rogan josh. Photos courtesy of the restaurants and Tripadvisor

picked.t: Vietnam ranks among world's top 10 for real estate transparency improvements
picked.body: Overall, Vietnam ranked 50th among 88 countries and territories surveyed, with a transparency score of 3.15, remaining in the Semi-Transparent category of JLL's 2026 Global Real Estate Transparency Index. JLL's index assesses real estate transparency across six areas: market performance measurement, governance and regulation, market fundamentals, transaction processes, governance of listed companies and sustainability. The Asia-Pacific region recorded the strongest gains in transparency, hosting five of the 10 most improved markets: India, Vietnam, South Korea, Australia and Thailand. Others in the top 10 included Poland, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Dubai and Abu Dhabi. JLL said the improvements had helped drive a recovery in cross-border investment in the region over the past 12 months, with direct investment transaction volumes in some markets, including Vietnam, reaching record levels. Before 2020, Vietnam was classified as a Low Transparency market, with limited market data and complex legal frameworks that created challenges for foreign property investors, according to JLL's data. A turning point came in 2016 when Vietnam joined the Trans-Pacific Partnership and proposed developing a national real estate database, signaling efforts to align the market with international standards. The country moved into the Semi-Transparent category in 2020. In 2024, Vietnam took a major step in strengthening its legal framework, as the revised laws on land, housing and real estate business came into effect. The revised Law on Price also introduced requirements for certified valuation professionals and verifiable audit trails for valuations, while regulations required real estate transactions to be conducted through the banking system. A new degree on the construction, management and operation of housing and real estate market information systems took effect this year, with the goal of completing the national land database by the end of 2026. The country has also seen greater adoption of sustainable development practices in the real estate sector. "The fact that Vietnam is ranked among the global top 10 markets with the strongest improvements in transparency is the result of a long and sustained process," said Le Thi Huyen Trang, JLL Vietnam's general director. Trang said reforms to the legal framework, administrative procedures and economic policy, have begun to produce positive results, reflected in rising registered foreign investment. She noted that Vietnam recorded US$38.1 billion in registered foreign investment in the first seven months of 2026, nearly matching the total registered FDI in the previous year and marking the highest level in a decade. JLL's report also highlighted a relationship between market transparency and the accuracy and efficiency of property valuations. In Semi-transparent markets such as Vietnam, fragmented and limited data mean valuation accuracy is estimated at around 70%, while the process can take up to 20 days. The accuracy is around 90% in Highly Transparent markets where transaction data is publicly available and comprehensive, with valuations typically taking five to 10 days. According to JLL, further progress towards greater transparency in Vietnam will depend on completing the digitization of land records, establishing a unified nationwide property registration system, applying international valuation standards and publishing data on commercial real estate credit markets. It also requires expanding green building certification, more comprehensive planning and reliable databases and stronger disclosure requirements for listed companies. JLL said greater transparency would become increasingly important for investors as economic and geopolitical uncertainty, artificial intelligence, shifting capital flows, energy security and changes in real estate credit markets reshape investment decision-making worldwide.

picked.t: Chance reunion sparks whirlwind cross-continental romance for Vietnamese artist
picked.body: In February 2026, Giang, 47, an instructor at the Versailles Conservatory in France, traveled to Australia to visit relatives. At a party, she noticed a man looking intently at her. Quickly, she recognized him as Richard Horne, 50, the director of a center that helps people with disabilities find employment. The two had met at another party in Australia two years earlier, when they sat at the same table but left without exchanging contact information. Each continued to ask a mutual friend about the other. "I’m shy by nature and rarely make the first move, but when we met again, I told myself I couldn’t let the opportunity pass a second time," Horne said. The following evening, they had dinner at an intimate European-style restaurant and talked nonstop. As they discovered how much they had in common, Horne asked, "How did we go more than 40 years without meeting? Where have you been all this time?" Giang took the remark as a declaration that he intended to pursue her. Since she was due to leave Australia in five days, he took time off work and drove more than 370 miles to join her family on a vacation farther south. His persistence earned him another date and an opportunity to ask Giang’s parents for permission to court her formally. After she returned to France, Horne sent her a handwritten letter every week, sometimes running to 10 pages. He wrote on perfume-scented, vintage-style stationery reminiscent of aristocratic correspondence. Flowers and souvenirs also arrived regularly at her home, accompanied by the message, "Home is where you are." He told her he had not written anything by hand in 20 years, but love inspired him to start again. Their budding relationship soon met resistance from Giang’s 13-year-old daughter, Xuan An. Her father had been absent from her life since she was six months old. Though she initially supported her mother’s decision to date, she reacted strongly when she realized the relationship was serious. "Mom, don’t ever get married again," she said. "No matter who you marry, you’ll get hurt." Horne understood that An feared losing her mother. He did not pressure her to accept him, but wanted her to understand that no one would take her place in Giang’s life. He wrote An a separate letter asking for permission to become part of both their lives. For her birthday, he gave her $50 and a bracelet with a note: "Because I’m far away, I can’t take your mother out for coffee. Please use this money to take her out for a drink, and keep whatever is left as spending money." The gesture softened An’s attitude, though she still balked at having a man she barely knew stay in their home. When she learned that Horne planned to visit Paris and hoped to stay with them to better understand their daily lives, she issued an ultimatum. "Either he stays at a hotel, or I’ll move out and let him stay here," she told her mother. Drawing on his experience raising two children to adulthood, Horne tried another approach: He asked An to help him choose an engagement ring for her mother. Being entrusted with such an important decision made the teenager feel respected. When Horne visited Paris in April, he went to the theater over three days to hear An perform on the violin. His patience finally earned him her acceptance. One day in mid-April, Horne got down on one knee and proposed to Giang at the Temple of Love in Versailles, with their friends looking on. That evening, they celebrated over dinner aboard a boat on the Seine, complete with a cake and love songs. Their engagement raised a practical question: Where would they live? Horne was prepared to leave the life he had built in Australia and move to France, but he spoke no French and would have struggled to find work. Giang had a stable career and students in France, but she also longed for a change of scenery. One colleague reminded her that "happiness won’t wait." The conservatory’s director promised her that she would be welcome to return if life in Australia did not suit her. Encouraged by the support, Giang asked for a year of unpaid leave. With a late-July wedding approaching, the couple raced to organize their new life in opposite hemispheres. In France, Giang wrapped up her work. In Australia, Horne handled the visa paperwork, prepared her résumé and searched for jobs on her behalf. He also found a school for An, renovated the house, and organized the wedding. Giang said many friends their age chose to live with new partners without remarrying after previous relationships ended, but she and Horne both wanted to formalize their commitment through marriage. "At this age, I understand that meeting someone and falling in love are only the beginning. Love takes understanding and effort to grow." Giang has since received two teaching offers in Australia and plans to develop cultural projects for the community. Each evening, the three of them rehearse "Bonjour Vietnam" (Hello Vietnam) in three languages for a cultural event in November.

picked.t: 11 most beautiful destinations in Vietnam, according to UK newspaper
picked.body: It recently published an article by travel writer Joshua Zukas, showcasing the destinations and recommending experiences for foreigner visitors. Hue tops the list. The former imperial capital draws travelers with its lush urban spaces, tree-lined avenues, parks along the Huong River, and rich heritage, including the Imperial City, Hue garden houses, and lotus ponds. Unlike bustling Hoi An, Hue offers a tranquil vibe, ideal for those interested in exploring Nguyen Dynasty history and architecture. Visitors can take a boat ride on the Huong River, explore the Imperial City and royal tombs, and savor the traditional local cuisine. Photo by Vo Thanh Hanoi's old quarter is also featured in the list and described as an area that reflects the capital's daily pace of life. The old quarter is a dense maze of narrow alleys, shops, and street food stalls, interspersed with French colonial architecture, ancient temples, and pagodas. Travelers are encouraged to explore on foot to fully experience the area, strolling through specialized craft streets, sampling street food and sidewalk coffee, and discovering historic French-style villas hidden deep within the alleyways. Photo by Hoang Giang The British publication said while Sa Pa is experiencing rapid tourism growth, the surrounding countryside retains its natural beauty, defined by rolling hills, mountain ranges, and terraced rice fields. Pictured is the O Quy Ho tea hill in Sa Pa in December 2025. Travelers seeking an authentic, unspoiled mountain experience are advised to join trekking tours through local villages and stay at locals' houses to immerse themselves in regional culture. Photo by Hoang Trung Hieu Hoang Su Phi in Tuyen Quang Province is described as an ideal destination to escape the crowds. It has dramatic terraced rice fields clinging to steep mountain slopes. Visitors can travel by motorbike or car to admire these iconic terraces during the watering season or the golden harvest season. Photo by Pham Hoang Cuong Cao Bang captivates visitors with its karst landscapes, river networks, and iconic landmarks such as Ban Gioc waterfall (pictured) and Thung mountain (also known as God's Eye mountain). The region preserves its rich historical and cultural heritage, including the Khuoi Ky stone village. Travelers can rent cars or motorbikes to drive through the mountain passes, explore waterfalls, and visit historical sites. Photo by Thai Duong AC Phong Nha - Ke Bang national park is renowned for its ancient karst landscape and vast cave system. The place has an array of caves ranging from easily accessible spots to complex subterranean networks. Visitors can take a boat trip to explore Phong Nha Cave, walk through Paradise Cave (Thien Duong), or sign up for adventure expeditions to Son Doong, the world's largest cave, En Cave, and Va Cave. Pictured is a newly discovered cave in Phong Nha - Ke Bang, photographed in June. Photo by Jungle Boss The coastline of the south-central region also finds a place in the list of Vietnam's 11 most beautiful destinations. The coastal route connecting Quy Nhon and Phan Rang is dotted with by rocky peninsulas, secluded coves, fine sandy beaches, and crystal-clear waters. Pictured is a 115 km stretch of the coastal road passing through Quy Nhon. Travelers can explore this scenic coastal drive by car or motorbike, stopping along the way to visit fishing villages and pristine, untouched beaches. Photo by Nguyen Gia My Son sanctuary in Da Nang is introduced as a site of ancient beauty, housing a complex of historic Champa temples constructed between the 4th and 13th centuries. Visitors are advised to explore the sanctuary early in the morning to beat the heat and avoid large crowds, and take the opportunity to learn about the history of Champa architecture. Photo by heritagewanderlust Another destination in Da Nang featured on the list is the Son Tra peninsula. Known as the "green shield" protecting the city from strong winds, the area is home to the rare red-shanked douc langur (pictured). Visitors are recommended to ride motorbikes along the coastal road around Bac Beach, visit Linh Ung Pagoda, and go on wildlife watching tours. Photo by Ngo Tran Hai An Cat Tien national park, recognized by UNESCO as a world biosphere reserve, is home to hundreds of rare animal species. More than just a destination for exploration, it is also a peaceful retreat for nature lovers. The British newspaper suggested that travelers should trek through the jungle, mountain bike, visit the Bau Sau (crocodile lake) area, and join night wildlife safaris. Photo by Tang A Pau Con Dao is a distinct getaway thanks to its pristine nature and slow pace of life. Beyond its rich historical and spiritual significance, the archipelago stands out as an eco-tourism destination, with over 80% of its land area covered by a national park. Home to luxury international resort brands, it has repeatedly featured on the global travel map. Photo by Linh Huynh

picked.t: Vietnamese student gives up Western plans to follow his sister to 'China's MIT'
picked.body: Nguyen Khoa Vu, a graduate of Hanoi's Foreign Language Specialized School, has won a 50% tuition scholarship to Tsinghua University's Zhishan College. Tsinghua, often dubbed "China's MIT", ranks 14th in the QS World University Rankings 2027. Zhishan, a social sciences college Tsinghua launched in 2024, charges CNY26,000 (US$3,900) a year in tuition. Its majors include economics, sociology, political science and public administration, international politics and statistics. Vu's older sister, Nguyen Vu Tue Giang, was admitted to Tsinghua on a scholarship in 2025. Used to Western culture and passionate about basketball, Vu flatly refused when his mother suggested he follow his sister to Beijing. "At one point I told my parents straight out: "either the U.K. or the U.S., or I stay home," he recalled. In August 2025, he traveled to Beijing with his family for his sister's enrollment. The modern classrooms, swimming pool and basketball courts, along with time spent with Vietnamese students there, won him over. "Everything felt right, and I realized this was the environment for me," he said. Vu's application included his transcripts, language certificates, recommendation letters, a personal essay and a self-introduction video. He also submitted math and Chinese results from the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA), a new standardized test for international undergraduate applicants. He kept an average above 9 out of 10 throughout high school. His language scores include IELTS 7.5 and HSK 6, the highest of the Chinese proficiency test's six core levels. In his essay, Vu wrote about setting aside his dream of playing professional basketball to focus on academics and economics. "I wanted to show that however passionate I am about sports, I can set it aside and excel at another goal," he said. "A sports career is a huge challenge because it requires substantial resources and the right environment to develop," he added. He picked economics because he inherited his mother's head for business, he said. While still in school, he imported trendy toys and sold sneakers online. After clearing the application review, Vu advanced to an in-person interview. Three professors spent 15 minutes questioning him on a range of topics and even had him solve math problems on the spot. Candidates must keep the interview content confidential. "At one point I admitted I didn't know anything about a topic the professor raised and asked for a different question," Vu said, crediting honesty for his success. Vu handled pressure remarkably well, moving from HSK 4 to HSK 6 in six months, said Hoang Lan Chi, a lecturer at Hanoi's University of Languages and International Studies who guided him through the application. "Vu proved he meets the university's admission criteria. He is well-rounded, from academics, music and sports to determination, perseverance and discipline," she said. Giang, self-motivated and a natural student, mostly needed support from the sidelines, said their mother, Mai Dung. Vu was capable but sometimes distracted, she said, so she watched him more closely, often pointing to successful role models and steering him toward his sister's example. "I let my children experience things, take responsibility and face failure early, while quietly creating situations that spark their passion," she said.
